title: Knowledge Check 4: Lessons 16-20
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 16-20 of the ai-at-work series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: What is an AI tool's real strength in a problem-solving task?
options: Choosing the best option from a set
Generating a wide range of options for you to judge
Confirming in advance which plan will succeed
Replacing your judgment about what to do
questions.explanation: The tool produces options quickly and cannot reliably tell which one is good. That split is the point: it widens the field, and the choosing stays with you.

questions.question: When comparing options, what is the honest way to weigh a tradeoff?
options: Compare only the total cost of each option
Pick whichever option feels safest and move on
Ask what each option costs, risks, and assumes
Go with whichever option the tool recommends first
questions.explanation: Every real option costs something, risks something, and assumes something. Naming all three is what makes the comparison real instead of trusting a gut pick.

questions.question: What does a premortem ask you to do before committing to a plan?
options: List the tasks the plan still has to complete
Estimate the plan's total budget and timeline
Review the plan after it has finished
Imagine the plan has already failed and work back to why
questions.explanation: A premortem flips a vague question about what could go wrong into a specific answer by imagining the failure first. That surfaces risks while they are still cheap to fix.

questions.question: Why is 'can the tool do this?' the wrong first question when you decide whether to delegate a task?
options: Because the tool's answer depends on how the prompt is worded
Because the answer is almost always yes, which tells you nothing about whether you should use it
Because a tool's abilities change with every software update
Because money is the only factor that should decide the choice
questions.explanation: The tool can produce a draft or a list for nearly anything you describe, so a yes to can-I is nearly automatic. The better question is should-I, because it forces you to weigh the task itself.

questions.question: A tool wrote the words, but the result is a commitment a client will hold you to. Who is accountable for it?
options: The vendor, since their model produced the work
No one, because a tool cannot be held responsible
You are, because a tool has no reputation, job, or relationship to protect
Whoever was in the room when it was sent
questions.explanation: A tool cannot be accountable for anything, so whenever a task ends in something you own, the accountability stays with you. That single fact drives most of the decision about whether to delegate.

questions.question: You could write a short reply yourself in a few moments. Why might using the tool still be the wrong call?
options: Because short replies are not something a tool can produce
Because the tool would refuse such a small request
Because the tool would ask for more context first
Because prompting, reading, and fixing the output can cost more time than just writing it
questions.explanation: Using a tool is never free. For a small task, the time to prompt, read, and correct the output can exceed the task itself, so the tool is not worth using even when it can do the work.

questions.question: Why is asking whether your whole job is automatable the wrong starting question?
options: It is a question only a manager can answer
A job is a bundle of tasks, and only some of them suit a tool
It assumes automation always means writing code
It is too pessimistic to lead anywhere useful
questions.explanation: Almost every job mixes judgment with repeatable work. Asking which tasks qualify is narrow enough to act on, while the whole-job question has no useful answer.

questions.question: Which of these is a rule-based task rather than a judgment call?
options: Deciding whether to waive a late fee for a long-standing client
Choosing which supplier to keep after a price dispute
Sending the standard reminder when an invoice passes its due date
Setting next quarter's targets for the team
questions.explanation: A rule-based task has steps you could write down and hand over without being asked a single question. The others turn on context, relationships, or consequences that stay with you.

questions.question: A task runs twice a year and takes an hour each time. What does the frequency signal suggest?
options: It is a strong candidate because the steps are predictable
It should be automated first because errors are easy to spot
Frequency does not matter if the task is rule-based
It is rarely worth the setup, because the return is small
questions.explanation: Automation is an investment and frequency is the return. A task you run a few times a year usually costs more to set up than it ever saves.

questions.question: What turns a pile of saved prompts into an actual library?
options: Storing them in a dedicated app
Collecting as many prompts as possible
Metadata on each prompt: a name, a when-to-use line, and a what-to-check note
Writing each prompt as a formal template
questions.explanation: Without metadata, saved prompts are just text you cannot find again. A name, a when-to-use line, and a what-to-check note are what let you reach the right prompt in seconds.

questions.question: A saved prompt is worth keeping when it is a working prompt. What makes a prompt a working prompt?
options: It already produced an output you used and were happy with
It follows a formal template with placeholders
It was written by a colleague rather than you
It is long and highly detailed
questions.explanation: A working prompt has been tested in your real job and produced output you used, which is what makes the library trustworthy instead of a collection of untried ideas.

questions.question: What should never be stored in a prompt library?
options: Prompts you use only twice a year
Confidential details such as real customer data
Prompts with placeholders for missing values
Short prompts for small recurring tasks
questions.explanation: A library holds the shape of a prompt and its blanks, not the secrets that go in them. Keeping confidential data out keeps the library safe to open anywhere.

questions.question: What turns a single prompt into a workflow?
options: Running the same prompt more than once
A fixed sequence of steps, run in order, that feeds a recurring result
Using a more capable model
Saving the prompt somewhere you can find it again
questions.explanation: A prompt is one request, while a workflow is several steps arranged so each one hands its output to the next. The order and the handoffs are what make it a routine.

questions.question: What is the role of the final check in a workflow?
options: It speeds up the drafting steps
It replaces the need for saved prompts
It is where you verify the output before it leaves your hands
It only runs until the workflow proves stable, then stops
questions.explanation: The check is where the human decides, and it is the step never skipped. A routine that ships output nobody verified is delegation, not a safe workflow.

questions.question: Why should a weekly workflow get a fixed time budget?
options: A routine you can finish in a set window actually runs every week, while one that sprawls gets skipped
It makes the tool's output more accurate
It stops the tool from running for too long
It is how the subscription is billed
questions.explanation: A workflow is a habit, and habits survive when they stay small. A set window keeps it bounded enough to run every week instead of ballooning into a task you keep skipping.
